chapter: Sue and Patsy Howard in show business
title: Patsy on the Ellington revue Jump for Joy
summary: Patsy describes dancing and assistant choreography in Jump for Joy: the cast, three-month run and its social-consciousness numbers.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: Patsy, can you answer a question, dear? We hit on a spot here that, if you'd like, you could help us. You were involved with 'Jump for Joy', weren't you?
I was --
Can you come in here a minute, because we're trying to get everybody in here, now, if you don't mind, yeah, because we knew that you had to be there. Yeah, just a
couple of points, because we want this to be put in right form. Sooner or later, we can all okay it later, but why don't you ask her --
You danced in 'Jump for Joy'?
Yeah. No -- well, I did dance in it, but I was assistant choreographer also for 'Jump for Joy'.
Who was the choreographer?
Well, there was Nick Castle, who had -- he was formerly with Paramount Studios and Columbia different Studios, but mostly with Paramount.
So you worked with the Ellington band and who all else was in that --
Marie Bryant and Dorothy Dandridge and Pot Pan and Skillet. Ivy Anderson started out there, and let me see who else.
Herb Jeffries?
What?
Herb Jeffries?
Herb Jeffries, yes, he was one of the stars. And the Rockets, was a dance trio.
Who was in that? Who were the --
They were called the Rockets. It was Baby Face -- they called him Baby Face Robertson, Johnny Thomas and Andrew Jackson.
And how was the show put together?
I've been told that at some point it was revised or it was revised a lot or --

No, it was never revised. I mean, we had had -- of course, they had eyes for Broadway, and after it opened here, everyone thought it was going to Broadway, but it didn't do it. It didn't even get -- it only played here, L.A.
But I understand it was very, very successful.
It was, very successful.
Three months?
Just about three months.
I'd heard that the reason it did not go on was that there was some kind of dispute over who got the publishing rights to the music, and because of that this kind of --

Well, that could have been because there's quite a few that was -- and, like, Sid Culler, who is -- I think he writes Studio and different things, and I can't think who else, but there was quite a few involved in 'Jump for Joy.'
Somebody said John Garfield had something to do with staging some of the --
No, he didn't, no.
I think Barney Bogard told me that.
Well, I don't know, maybe it might have been when we weren't around, doing the musical numbers, because they had different sketches and skits and things like that.
How did you feel about the show?

Oh, I thought it was -- yes, it was beautiful, I thought. Of course, it was at the time when everything was trying to bring out some of the racial stuff, like, one of the numbers was 'Uncle Tom's Cabin is a Drive-in Now,' and -- well, 'Jump for Joy,' the lyrics, and -- I forgot, this is --
"Sun-Tan Is One-Tenth of the Nation." (Inaudible.)
Right, Brown-Skinned Gal in the Calico Gown, and it was beautiful. It was a beautiful show.
And Duke used to refer to it as a social consciousness musical.
Yes.
How about reviews of it at the time?
Well, it had successful reviews, really nice.
It was a whole different kind --
Kind of a show, really.
-- than had been done before.
Before, un-huh, right.
So it wasn't a Shuffle Along, --
No, no.
A whole new approach, and --
A whole new concept of everything.
Everybody felt so good.
Yeah, beautiful about it.
